hints: Compare the direction in which particles are displaced with the direction in which wave energy travels.
walkthrough: A transverse wave transfers energy in the direction in which the wave travels.
The particles do not move along that direction; their displacement is at right angles to it.
Therefore, in a transverse wave, particle displacement is perpendicular to the direction of energy propagation.

ai_rubric.observable: States that particle displacement is perpendicular to the direction of energy propagation.

hints: State what happens when waves overlap and how the resultant displacement is found.
walkthrough: First identify the situation: two or more waves meet or overlap at the same point.
At that point, each wave contributes its own displacement.
The resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements.
This statement is the principle of superposition.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the waves meet or overlap at a point.
States that the resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements.

hints: Use the wave speed and period directly: one period is the time taken for one wavelength to pass.
walkthrough: Use the wave relationship v = fλ together with f = 1/T.
This gives λ = vT.
Substitute v = 4.0 cm s⁻¹ and T = 1.5 s: λ = 4.0 × 1.5.
Calculate λ = 6.0 cm.
The wavelength of the water waves is 6.0 cm.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses λ = vT, or uses λ = v/f together with f = 1/T.

hints: Calculate the path difference PR − QR and express it as a number of wavelengths.
An odd number of half-wavelengths gives waves in antiphase at R.
walkthrough: Calculate the path difference: PR − QR = 44 cm − 29 cm = 15 cm.
From part (b)(i), the wavelength is 6.0 cm.
Express the path difference in wavelengths: 15 ÷ 6.0 = 2.5 wavelengths.
A path difference of 2.5λ is an odd number of half-wavelengths, so the waves arrive 180° out of phase.
The waves from P and Q have equal amplitudes at R, so their opposite displacements cancel completely.
Destructive interference therefore occurs and the water particles are at rest at R.

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates the path difference as 15 cm = 2.5λ.
Recognises that 2.5λ gives a phase difference of 180°, or is of the form (n + ½)λ.
Concludes that destructive interference makes the resultant displacement zero at R.

hints: Read the amplitudes at x = 2.0 cm and x = 10.0 cm from the graph.
Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, so square the amplitude ratio.
walkthrough: From the graph, the amplitude at x = 2.0 cm is approximately 0.90 cm, so A₁ = 0.90 cm.
At x = 10.0 cm, the amplitude is approximately 0.60 cm, so A₂ = 0.60 cm.
For a progressive wave, intensity is proportional to amplitude squared.
Therefore I₂/I₁ = A₂²/A₁² = (0.60/0.90)².
To two significant figures, I₂/I₁ = 0.44.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses intensity proportional to amplitude squared.
Uses amplitudes of approximately 0.60 cm and 0.90 cm to obtain I₂/I₁ = 0.44.

hints: Read the wavelength from the distance between neighbouring crests, then compare the 1.0 cm separation with that wavelength.
walkthrough: The distance between neighbouring crests is approximately 4.0 cm, so the wavelength is λ = 4.0 cm.
The two positions are separated by Δx = 4.0 cm − 3.0 cm = 1.0 cm.
The separation is therefore Δx/λ = 1.0/4.0 = ¼ of a wavelength.
One complete wavelength corresponds to 360°, so the phase difference is ¼ × 360°.
Calculate the phase difference: ¼ × 360° = 90°.
The phase difference is 90 degrees.

ai_rubric.observable: States a phase difference of 90° with a valid angular unit.
